## Author's thesis (paraphrased from source)

The handbook is an introductory, selective collection of software engineering methods: pre-established ways to achieve specific objectives that may help save a project. It does not promise to teach the reader how to *be* a software engineer or to cover the whole field; it aims to help readers judge whether a topic or method is relevant, gain enough understanding to discuss it, and find a starting point for further exploration. [AR] (Introduction, pp. 1–3, "What’s This Book Like?")

> I won’t tell you how to be a software engineer; you’ll learn that over time by doing it.
>
> [V] (Introduction, p. 1)

The author presents software engineering as contextual and changeable rather than a domain of reproducible black-and-white answers. What a practitioner needs depends on the situation, many topics are best learned on the job, and a useful short handbook should therefore introduce methods with guidance about when and why to use them rather than attempt exhaustive coverage. [AR] (Introduction, pp. 2–3, "What’s the Philosophy Behind This Book?")

The practical end is software that solves problems people care about while remaining sustainable and extensible: feasible to keep running, maintain, grow, and extend with features. [AP] (Introduction, p. 2, "What’s the Purpose of Software Engineering?") The handbook favours Agile because of its popularity and the author's experience, while explicitly declining to treat Agile as perfect or universally final. [AP] (Introduction, pp. 2–3, "Agile Isn’t Perfect, But I Really Like It")

Across the eight topics, a common method runs beneath the particulars: make work and expectations visible, communicate at a level suited to the audience, gather feedback before commitments become expensive, expose uncertainty and dependencies, and revise designs, plans, or code as evidence accumulates. [AR] (Ch 1, pp. 7–13; Ch 2, pp. 15–29; Ch 3, pp. 31–44; Ch 4, pp. 46–58; Ch 6, pp. 69–72; Ch 8, pp. 85–93)

## Part I: Framing software engineering and method choice

### Software engineering and the handbook's boundaries

The glossary defines software engineering as the systematic application of scientific and technological knowledge, methods, and experience to software design, implementation, testing, and documentation, borrowing the definition from the ISO/IEC/IEEE vocabulary standard. [BT] (Glossary, p. 100, "software engineering"; Introduction, p. 1, "What’s Software Engineering?")

The handbook defines a method as a pre-established way of achieving a specific outcome. [AP] (Glossary, p. 98, "method") Its selection principle is contextual: a method is valuable when it fits the project's objective and circumstances, not because the book treats it as a universal prescription. [AR] (Introduction, pp. 1–3, "What’s the Philosophy Behind This Book?")

The second edition moved the text from PDF/LaTeX to HTML/CSS, added alternative text, brought references, figures, and tables into APA style, added more inline citations, and revised several chapters substantively. [AP] (Introduction, pp. 4–5, "What’s New in the Second Edition?")

### The eight-topic learning path

The author enumerates eight major topics and assigns each a distinct practical purpose: [AP] (Introduction, p. 3, "What’s This Book Like?")

1. **Agile** — a collaboration-oriented philosophy that values doing over comprehensive planning and documentation. [AP] (Introduction, p. 3)
2. **Project Management and Teamwork** — organised work with other people. [AP] (Introduction, p. 3)
3. **Requirements** — clarity about what the software is expected to do. [AP] (Introduction, p. 3)
4. **UML class and sequence diagrams** — diagrams for communicating how code works or should work. [AP] (Introduction, p. 3)
5. **Monolith versus microservice architectures** — contrasting high-level ways to organise code. [AP] (Introduction, p. 3)
6. **Paper prototyping** — designing a user interface before coding it. [AP] (Introduction, p. 3)
7. **Inclusivity Heuristics** — designing for people unlike the designer. [AP] (Introduction, p. 3)
8. **Code smells and refactoring** — improving code so it is easier to work with. [AP] (Introduction, p. 3)

The count is eight, matching both the author's numbered list and the eight numbered chapters in the contents. [AP] (Contents, pp. 7–93; Introduction, p. 3)

## Part II: Agile, Scrum, and development cycles

### Five SDLC stages and contrasting process models

The software development life cycle is presented as five stages: requirements, design, implementation, testing, and maintenance. Requirements determine what the software must do and under what constraints; design determines code structure and user interaction; implementation turns requirements and design into code; testing covers verification and validation; maintenance improves existing functionality and code. [AP] (Ch 1, pp. 7–8, "1.1 The Software Development Life Cycle")

The source contrasts patterns for moving through those five stages. Agile uses relatively short, numerous cycles and frequent incremental releases, while Waterfall is comparatively linear, sequential, and documentation-heavy. [AP] (Ch 1, pp. 8–9, "1.1 The Software Development Life Cycle") The author notes the irony that Royce's 1970 article, often associated with Waterfall, describes the simple downward model's major flaws and later proposes feedback and preliminary design. [BT] (Ch 1, pp. 8–9, "1.1 The Software Development Life Cycle")

The practical reasons to learn process models and methods are to recognise what a team is doing, enlarge the set of approaches available when choosing a process, and have options when a project is in trouble. [AP] (Ch 1, pp. 9–10, "1.1.1 Why Care about Agile")

### Agile prevalence and reported outcomes

The handbook treats Agile as a philosophy without a single concrete implementation; frameworks such as Scrum make the philosophy more operational. [AP] (Ch 1, p. 13, "1.3 Summary")

In an HP survey of 601 respondents, the reported primary-process distribution was 51% leaning Agile, 24% hybrid, 16% pure Agile, 7% leaning Waterfall, and 2% pure Waterfall; those five categories total 100%. [BT] (Ch 1, pp. 10–11, "1.2.1 Agile") Among 403 organisations primarily adopting Agile, the separately reported agreement rates were 54% for enhanced cross-team collaboration, 52% for increased software quality, 49% for increased customer satisfaction, 43% for shorter time to market, and 42% for reduced development cost. [BT] (Ch 1, p. 11, "1.2.1 Agile")

### Scrum's team, events, and artefacts

The handbook's compact Scrum account follows the Scrum Guide and organises the framework into three categories: team, events, and artefacts. [BT] (Ch 1, pp. 11–13, "1.2.2 Scrum")

The team has three named accountabilities: Scrum Master, Product Owner, and Developers. The source characterises their respective centres of attention as process, product value, and creating a usable Increment while following Scrum processes. [AP] (Ch 1, pp. 11–12, "1.2.2 Scrum")

The five events are the Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, and Sprint Retrospective. Sprints are fixed-length periods of one month or less; Planning lays out the work; the Daily Scrum is a 15-minute developer event; the Review inspects outcomes with stakeholders; and the Retrospective plans improvements to quality and effectiveness within the team. [BT] (Ch 1, p. 12, "1.2.2 Scrum")

The three artefacts are the Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, and Increment. The first is an ordered list of product-improvement needs; the second combines the Sprint Goal, selected Product Backlog items, and an actionable delivery plan; the third is a concrete step toward the Product Goal. [BT] (Ch 1, pp. 12–13, "1.2.2 Scrum")

Three example Agile methods round out the chapter: a Scrum board visualises work as cards in categorical columns; a spike is a focused investigation used to answer a question or choose a path; and a user story briefly describes functionality from the perspective of a user need. [AP] (Ch 1, p. 13, "1.2.3 Agile Methods")

## Part III: Project management, teamwork, and risk reduction

### Triple constraint, risk, and managerial skill mix

Project management is the planning and execution of a project while balancing time, cost, and scope. Time covers duration and intermediate deadlines; cost covers money, people, and other resources; scope covers objectives, requirements, and quality. [AP] (Ch 2, pp. 15–17, "2.2 Triple Constraint") Changing one constraint strategically generally requires a corresponding change in at least one other constraint. [BT] (Ch 2, p. 17, "2.2 Triple Constraint")

Risk is the estimated probability of loss given known and unknown factors. The chapter's mitigation repertoire includes defining and tracking the project, communicating with the team, researching decisions, preparing backup plans, and selecting suitable tools. [AP] (Ch 2, p. 15, "Project Management and Teamwork")

Badawy's managerial skill mix contains three categories: interpersonal, technical, and administrative/conceptual. The chapter concentrates on the first two because project managers often need direct communication and technical-method skills more than the macro-level emphasis typical of senior executives. [BT] (Ch 2, pp. 17–18, "2.3 Managerial Skill Mix")

### Communication methods

The chapter uses Tuckman's five-stage team-development model as background: forming, storming, norming, performing, and adjourning. [BT] (Ch 2, p. 18, "2.4 Interpersonal Skills: Team Communication")

> One way to reduce risk is to improve team communication
>
> [V] (Ch 2, p. 18, "2.4 Interpersonal Skills: Team Communication")

Ground rules can be created before conflict or revised in response to it. Effective rules require whole-team buy-in and may cover vision, priorities, routine communication, conflict communication, work habits, responsiveness, responses to unmet expectations, and ways of getting to know one another. [AP] (Ch 2, pp. 18–19, "2.4.1 Establishing Ground Rules") Rules that feel phoney, trivial, overly aspirational, inflexible, or authoritarian can undermine the exercise. [AP] (Ch 2, p. 19, "2.4.1 Establishing Ground Rules")

A RACI matrix gives four responsibility labels: Responsible does the work; Accountable approves it and ensures completion; Consulted offers advice; Informed receives status updates. One person may hold more than one label, and tasks may be grouped by phase. [AP] (Ch 2, pp. 19–21, "2.4.2 Defining Roles and Responsibilities: RACI Matrix") Making these assignments explicit reduces risks created by ambiguity or denial about who was meant to do what. [AR] (Ch 2, p. 21, "2.4.2 Defining Roles and Responsibilities: RACI Matrix")

Fist of five is a consensus method with six possible signals, from zero through five fingers: strong reject, reject, weak reject, weak accept, accept, and strong accept/champion. A signal of two or fewer can trigger discussion, revision, and another vote; the team decides its required consensus threshold. [AP] (Ch 2, pp. 21–22, "2.4.3 Measuring and Building Consensus")

### Defining, prioritising, estimating, and scheduling work

In Agile settings, scope emerges through task sets such as a Product Backlog or Sprint Backlog and may be summarised by an iteration goal. In other settings, a statement of work may explicitly record the objective, deliverables, milestones, technical requirements, limitations, and exclusions. [AP] (Ch 2, p. 22, "2.5.1 Project Scope")

A project priority matrix assigns each of the triple constraints one of three postures: **constrain** means it must not worsen; **enhance** means seek improvement; **accept** means it may worsen if necessary. The source's medical-device example constrains scope, tightly controls cost, and accepts schedule movement, illustrating that the appropriate balance follows the project's consequences and funding conditions. [AE] (Ch 2, pp. 22–24, "2.5.2 Balancing Constraints")

The four-cell Eisenhower matrix maps urgency and importance to **do**, **decide**, **delegate**, and **delete**. The author treats it as a first-pass tool that can conserve resources and protect important non-urgent work from being perpetually displaced by urgent tasks. [AP] (Ch 2, pp. 24–25, "2.5.3 Task Prioritization")

For finer-grained prioritisation, the source recommends asking an expert, running a spike, tracing dependencies, asking customers or users directly or indirectly, voting, or using pairwise comparison. A spike itself has three repeated steps: formulate a question; investigate through reading and experimentation; repeat until enough information has been gathered. [AP] (Ch 2, pp. 25–26, "2.5.4 Finer-Grained Prioritization")

The chapter presents two ways of expressing task size from Cohn's Agile-planning account: story points compare a task's relative size, while ideal days estimate focused days without other work or distractions. Velocity is the work completed in those units and should be adjusted as real performance tests initial estimates. [BT] (Ch 2, p. 26, "2.5.5 Estimation")

Planning poker makes estimation a private-then-shared group process. Each participant selects an estimate before reveal; differences become prompts for discussion, because high estimates may expose overlooked difficulty and low estimates may expose a more efficient approach. The cycle repeats until estimates are sufficiently consistent. [AP] (Ch 2, pp. 26–27, "2.5.5 Estimation")

A project network diagram is a left-to-right directed graph whose nodes are tasks and whose arrows show sequence or dependency. At minimum, each task must be distinct and its predecessors known; duration estimates make the representation more useful. [AP] (Ch 2, pp. 27–28, "2.5.6 Scheduling")

The source lists eight common task-management-system feature groups: task CRUD; names, descriptions, notes, comments, and attachments; list, board, or timeline views; project organisation; assignees and due dates; task status; email notifications; and tags, keywords, or categories. [AP] (Ch 2, pp. 28–29, "2.5.7 Task Management Systems")

## Part IV: Requirements as shared, testable expectations

### Functional and nonfunctional requirements

A software requirement is a rule the software must conform to: what it must do, how well it must do it, and the constraints or limits it must respect. [AP] (Ch 3, p. 31, "Requirements")

The source distinguishes two main types. A functional requirement specifies behaviour under stated conditions and answers what the software must do. A nonfunctional requirement specifies a property, characteristic, or constraint and answers how well the software must perform or what limitation it must respect. [BT] (Ch 3, pp. 31–32, "3.1 Types of Requirements")

Requirements help align design and implementation, keep multiple developers pursuing the same goal, constrain stakeholder drift, communicate with stakeholders, track the remaining work, and clarify what is genuinely necessary. [AP] (Ch 3, pp. 32–33, "3.2 Why Requirements Matter")

### Eleven listed standards for good requirements

The Texas Department of Information Resources set reproduced by the author contains eleven listed qualities: [BT] (Ch 3, p. 33, "3.3 What Makes a Good Requirement")

1. correct;
2. unambiguous;
3. complete;
4. consistent;
5. ranked for importance and/or stability;
6. verifiable or testable;
7. modifiable;
8. traceable;
9. cross-referenced to related earlier documents;
10. uniquely identifiable; and
11. organised for maximum readability. [BT] (Ch 3, p. 33, "3.3 What Makes a Good Requirement")

### Elicitation and professional judgement

Requirements elicitation combines detecting stakeholder wants and needs with professional judgement about which requirements deserve focus. Stakeholders may include clients, managers, users, governments, integrating-software developers, the development team, and the practitioner. [AP] (Ch 3, pp. 33–34, "3.4 Requirements Elicitation")

The source lists four detection methods: interviews, focus groups, lab studies, and exploratory research that immerses the practitioner in relevant people's and products' context. [AP] (Ch 3, p. 34, "3.4 Requirements Elicitation") It also lists five cautions for developer-led elicitation: stakeholders may lack expertise, may have poor ideas, may not know what they want, may want something harmful, and invariably communicate imperfectly because they are human. [AP] (Ch 3, pp. 34–35, "3.4 Requirements Elicitation")

### Quality attributes, constraints, and measurable thresholds

The chapter lists nine common quality attributes: maintainability, portability, reliability, efficiency, integrity, memorability, flexibility, interoperability, and reusability. Each can be turned into a scale so that a threshold makes the corresponding nonfunctional requirement testable. [AP] (Ch 3, pp. 35–36, "3.5.1 Quality Attributes")

The five listed constraint families limit technology choices, target platforms, what may change, how code may be written, and how data may be handled. The author distinguishes them conceptually from quality attributes by noting that constraints are often externally mandated while quality priorities may be chosen within the team. [AP] (Ch 3, pp. 36–37, "3.5.2 Constraints")

### User stories, acceptance criteria, and use cases

The source shows three functional-requirement formats: a direct action-result statement, a user story, and given-when-then. User stories centre a role, desired capability, and benefit; given-when-then incorporates context and is commonly used for acceptance criteria. [AP] (Ch 3, pp. 37–38, "3.6 Functional Requirements")

The INVEST mnemonic names six properties of a good user story: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, and Testable. [BT] (Ch 3, pp. 39–41, "3.6.1 User Stories") Acceptance criteria negotiate what must be true for the story to be done; the source demonstrates those criteria in given-when-then form and argues that automated tests are ideal where feasible. [AP] (Ch 3, pp. 41–42, "3.6.1 User Stories")

Use cases are the more formal alternative: structured descriptions of what a system must do during user interaction. Every use case has three required parts — name, actor or actors, and flow of events. [AP] (Ch 3, pp. 42–43, "3.6.2 Use Cases") The eight additional parts listed are identifier, preconditions, postconditions, business relevance, dependencies, extensions, priorities, and nonfunctional requirements. [AP] (Ch 3, p. 43, "Additional Parts of a Use Case")

Requirements specification is both the act of writing requirements and the document produced; a software requirements specification may contain both functional and nonfunctional requirements. [AP] (Ch 3, pp. 43–44, "3.7 Requirements Specification"; "3.8 Summary")

## Part V: UML as communication at an appropriate level of detail

### Planning and documenting with diagrams

Diagrams have two primary uses in the chapter: planning software before creation and describing software that already exists. In both cases they support communication and evaluation; generated diagrams can also reduce documentation-maintenance effort. [AP] (Ch 4, pp. 46–47, "4.1 How Diagrams Help")

> If your intended audience does not understand your diagram—or misunderstands it—your diagram has failed.
>
> [V] (Ch 4, p. 47, "4.2 What Diagrams Must Do Well")

UML is a family of graphical notations for software design and description, especially object-oriented systems. Different diagram types use different notations for different purposes. [AP] (Ch 4, p. 47, "4.3 What Is UML?") The source states that UML was first published in 1994, became an Object Management Group standard in 1997, became an ISO standard in 2005, and is currently at version 2. [AP] (Ch 4, p. 47, "4.3 What Is UML?")

### Benefits and limits of UML

The source lists five benefits: UML supports both design and description; forces structured thinking; provides views at different design levels; gives software professionals a common language; and communicates structure without requiring the audience to read code. [AP] (Ch 4, pp. 47–48, "4.4 Why Use UML?")

The three listed drawbacks are variation in notation, the time required to get notation right, and maintenance when the design changes. The author's governing criterion is communicative value: if drawing the diagram takes longer than explaining the code another way, it is not helping. [AP] (Ch 4, pp. 48–49, "4.5 Why NOT Use UML?")

### Class and sequence diagrams

A class diagram shows classes, their static relationships, properties, and operations. The notation introduced includes notes; class boxes; visibility symbols; association; direction; property names; source and target multiplicities; and inheritance. [AP] (Ch 4, pp. 49–52, "4.6 Class Diagrams"; "4.6.1 UML Class Diagram Notation")

A sequence diagram shows interactions between participants, usually for one use case or scenario. Participants may be objects, people, or databases; the source again subordinates strict convention to audience comprehension. [AP] (Ch 4, pp. 53–54, "4.7 Sequence Diagrams") The seven notation elements explicitly demonstrated are participant, lifeline, message, activation bar, return, self-call, and deletion. [AP] (Ch 4, pp. 54–57, "4.7.1 UML Sequence Diagram Notation")

The chapter's final qualifier is that each diagram type highlights part of a design and leaves other parts out; UML diagrams communicate with humans, not computers. [AP] (Ch 4, p. 57, "4.8 Summary")

## Part VI: Choosing between monolith and microservice architectures

### Definitions and six microservice characteristics

The chapter uses architecture to mean the software's all-encompassing, high-level code design. It deliberately narrows attention to monoliths and microservices so their differences can expose broader architectural concerns. [AP] (Ch 5, p. 60, "Monolith versus Microservice Architectures")

A monolith is one interconnected codebase that cannot easily be separated into independently useful components that run on their own. The author notes that this shape is common enough to arise without deliberate architectural planning. [AP] (Ch 5, pp. 60–61, "5.1 Monolith Architecture")

Microservices are separate applications, each running in its own process and capable of being individually useful. [AP] (Ch 5, p. 61, "5.2 Microservice Architecture") Following headings borrowed from Lewis and Fowler, the chapter develops six characteristics: [BT] (Ch 5, pp. 61–64, "5.2 Microservice Architecture")

1. **Smart end points and dumb pipes** — communication mechanisms stay simple while services process and translate messages. [AP] (Ch 5, p. 61)
2. **Componentisation via services** — independently replaceable and upgradeable units run in their own processes. [BT] (Ch 5, pp. 61–62)
3. **Organisation around business capabilities** — services align to the capacity to produce customer value, rather than only to technology layers. [BT] (Ch 5, pp. 62–63)
4. **Decentralised data management** — each service typically owns a database, improving decoupling and failure containment while introducing eventual consistency. [AP] (Ch 5, p. 63)
5. **Decentralised governance** — compatibility at interfaces permits different implementation technologies, though it increases the breadth of technologies and standards to maintain. [AP] (Ch 5, pp. 63–64)
6. **Design for failure** — distributed processes and technologies encourage service-specific monitoring, logging, and explicit failure behaviour. [AP] (Ch 5, p. 64)

### Trade-offs across six comparison questions

The author compares the two architectures along six explicit dimensions: communication, deployment, scaling, testing, upgrading, and database use. [AP] (Ch 5, pp. 64–65, "5.3 Monolith Compared to Microservices")

Microservice communication is standardised but usually networked, so it can be slower, less reliable, and less secure than direct calls within a monolith. Independent deployment, replication of only heavily used services, per-service testing, and per-service technology upgrades create flexibility; the trade is more distributed operational and compatibility work. [AP] (Ch 5, pp. 61–65, "5.2.2 Componentization via Services"; "5.3 Monolith Compared to Microservices")

A monolith may deploy as one unit, communicate directly, and centralise data administration and consistency. Those same properties can lengthen whole-system tests and deployments, require every replicated machine to support the entire system, and create a database bottleneck. [AP] (Ch 5, pp. 64–65, "5.3 Monolith Compared to Microservices")

### ODOT TOCS case study

The source's technical case concerns the Oregon Department of Transportation's statewide Transportation Operation Center System, which CASS began moving from a monolith toward microservices. Dispatch centres needed different home screens, while the monolith was difficult to decouple, deployed only a few times a year, put heavy pressure on one database, and depended on a .NET Framework stack that Microsoft had stopped updating after version 4.8. [AE] (Ch 5, pp. 66–67, "5.5 Case Study: Microservice Architecture")

The replacement home-screen architecture integrates with the remaining monolith through a gateway and an AMQP message broker; each service is a separate application with its own database. The Profile Service uses JSON because it fits that service better than the monolith's relational database. [AE] (Ch 5, pp. 66–67, "5.5 Case Study: Microservice Architecture")

The case does not establish that microservices are universally superior; it demonstrates a context in which independent technology choices, data stores, and deployment boundaries addressed specific constraints. [AR] (Ch 5, pp. 65–67, "5.4 Summary"; "5.5 Case Study")

## Part VII: Paper prototyping as early, low-cost learning

### Three prototype fidelities

UI prototyping iteratively depicts how an interface should look and how users should interact with it, based on requirements. The cost argument is that changing a drawing is often faster and easier than changing implemented code, so design problems can be found earlier. [AP] (Ch 6, p. 69, "Paper Prototyping")

The author uses three fidelity levels: low fidelity is a rough sketch suited to feedback on high-level features and large low-cost changes; medium fidelity is a more detailed illustration suited to small changes in accepted features; high fidelity is polished and suited to focused tweaks. [AP] (Ch 6, pp. 69–71, "Paper Prototyping") These are explicitly the author's working definitions in a field where definitions vary. [AP] (Ch 6, p. 69)

> A paper prototype is a hand-drawn sketch of a UI design that’s based on the software’s requirements.
>
> [V] (Ch 6, p. 71, "Paper Prototyping")

### Interaction and feedback

A paper prototype can be interactive rather than static: movable pieces, annotations, strings, or other simple materials can show available actions and their results. The author cautions that elaborate craft work is wasteful if a simpler sketch would communicate equally well, especially when feedback may invalidate the design. [AP] (Ch 6, pp. 71–72, "6.1 Showing Interaction")

For a paper-prototype session, a practitioner can present an entry screen, give the user a task or allow exploration, observe interactions, and swap or create drawings in response. A think-aloud protocol asks the user to voice actions, goals, questions, and dislikes during the session. [AP] (Ch 6, p. 72, "6.2 Showing Your Concept to Others")

The chapter's synthesis is cost and communication: early prototype feedback can expose UI flaws before implementation and help teams, clients, and users discuss the intended software. [AP] (Ch 6, p. 72, "6.3 Summary")

## Part VIII: Inclusivity Heuristics and cognitive-style diversity

### Five cognitive facets and three personas

The Inclusivity Heuristics are guidelines for designing technology to work well across diverse users. The source relates them to inclusive design, which includes and learns from a broad range of human perspectives. [BT] (Ch 7, p. 73, "Inclusivity Heuristics")

The current heuristics address five cognitive facets involved in first-time technology use: attitude toward risk, computer self-efficacy, information-processing style, learning style, and motivations. Each facet is a spectrum rather than a single user type. [BT] (Ch 7, pp. 73–74, "Inclusivity Heuristics")

The chapter frames those facets through three personas — Abi, Pat, and Tim — with differing cognitive styles. In the examples, Abi is comparatively risk-averse, process-oriented, and lower in computer self-efficacy; Pat is moderately self-efficacious, cautious, and a mindful tinkerer; Tim is comparatively risk-tolerant, highly self-efficacious, technologically motivated, and inclined to tinker. [AP] (Ch 7, pp. 74–82, "7.2 Inclusivity Heuristics Personas"; "7.3 The Inclusivity Heuristics")

The heuristics are intended for heuristic evaluation: multiple evaluators independently inspect a design, record issues, compare findings, and combine the issue set. [BT] (Ch 7, p. 74, "7.1 Background")

### The eight heuristics

The source enumerates exactly eight Inclusivity Heuristics: [AP] (Ch 7, pp. 75–83, "7.3 The Inclusivity Heuristics"; "7.4 Summary")

1. **Explain the benefits of new and existing features.** This lets task-focused or risk-averse users judge relevance while still surfacing interesting functionality for exploratory users. [AP] (Ch 7, pp. 75–76)
2. **Explain the costs of new and existing features.** Time, effort, and configuration costs help users decide whether to proceed. [AP] (Ch 7, p. 76)
3. **Let users gather as much information as they want, and no more.** Comprehensive processors can inspect detail while selective users can move quickly. [AP] (Ch 7, pp. 76–77)
4. **Keep familiar features available.** Familiar paths reduce risk and self-blame without blocking exploration. [AP] (Ch 7, pp. 78–79)
5. **Make undo/redo and backtracking available.** Reversibility reassures cautious users and supports recovery by tinkerers. [AP] (Ch 7, pp. 79–80)
6. **Provide an explicit path through the task.** Process-oriented users receive structure while tinkerers can retain optional paths. [AP] (Ch 7, pp. 80–81)
7. **Provide ways to try out different approaches.** Alternatives and human help provide recovery paths when a method fails. [AP] (Ch 7, pp. 81–82)
8. **Encourage tinkerers to tinker mindfully.** Design cues can reduce mistakes and long distractions without removing exploration. [AP] (Ch 7, pp. 82–83)

The set is pluralistic rather than a prescription to optimise for only one persona: the design aim is to support the full range represented across each cognitive facet. [AR] (Ch 7, pp. 73–83)

## Part IX: Code smells, refactoring, and technical debt

### Why smells matter

Code smells indicate that code may need reorganisation and may be undergoing code decay. The opening examples include embarrassment about showing code, desire to rewrite from scratch, repeated effort to understand it, comments that no longer match, duplicated code, and coupling that makes one change break several others. [AP] (Ch 8, pp. 85–86, "Code Smells and Refactoring")

The author gives three reasons to act: smelly code is harder to maintain, tends to license more smelly code, and accumulates technical debt that can reduce productivity or ultimately contribute to project failure. [AP] (Ch 8, p. 86, "8.1 Why Care about Code Smells?")

Refactoring improves code without changing what the code does and is presented as a way to pay down technical debt. [AP] (Ch 8, pp. 86–87, "8.2 Your Code Stinks—Now What?")

### Eleven listed smells and responses

The chapter groups its coverage into comment smells, function smells, and general code smells. Its summary enumerates eleven specific smell-response pairs: [AP] (Ch 8, pp. 87–93, "8.3 Comments"; "8.4 Functions"; "8.5 Code"; "8.6 Summary")

1. **Obsolete comment** — remove or update it. [AP] (Ch 8, p. 88)
2. **Commented-out code** — remove it; use backup or version control if needed. [AP] (Ch 8, p. 88)
3. **Redundant comment** — remove it. [AP] (Ch 8, p. 88)
4. **Long comment** — simplify the code and shorten or remove the comment. [AP] (Ch 8, pp. 88–89)
5. **Long function** — split it; the source's rule of thumb is more than about ten lines, with five or fewer as an aim. [AP] (Ch 8, p. 89)
6. **Function with many jobs** — split it into functions with coherent responsibilities. [AP] (Ch 8, pp. 89–90)
7. **Function with many parameters** — combine parameters in an object, obtain data inside the function, or split the function; the source flags more than four, while noting some use more than three. [AP] (Ch 8, p. 90)
8. **Duplicate code** — consolidate it while avoiding unwanted dependencies. [AP] (Ch 8, pp. 91–92)
9. **Long lines** — break them up, replace detail with a function call, or introduce variables; the source's rule of thumb is more than about 100 characters. [AP] (Ch 8, pp. 91–92)
10. **Inconsistent conventions** — follow the project's existing conventions or establish consistent ones for a new project. [AP] (Ch 8, p. 92)
11. **Vague naming** — rename for communicative clarity, even when the resulting name is long. [AP] (Ch 8, pp. 92–93)

The comment discussion rejects both extremes: absent comments and excessive comments. Comments age separately from code, routine comments can hide important ones, and heavy commenting can be evidence that the code itself should become more self-explanatory. [AR] (Ch 8, pp. 87–88, "8.3.1 Drawbacks of Having Many Comments")

The chapter closes by tying refactoring back to the book's purpose: cleaner code supports sustainable, extensible software and makes collaboration easier. [AP] (Ch 8, p. 93, "8.6 Summary"; Introduction, p. 2, "What’s the Purpose of Software Engineering?")

## Positions the author explicitly frames against

- **Software engineering as black and white.** The author says right answers can be difficult to find and may not transfer across contexts, while the field changes with research, technology, methods, and the outside world. [AP] (Introduction, p. 2, "Software Engineering Is Not Black and White")
- **Exhaustive study as a prerequisite for useful practice.** Context changes what a person needs to know, an exhaustive treatment would be unwieldy, and many topics are better learned on the job. [AR] (Introduction, pp. 2–3, "It’s Not Necessary to Study Every Detail")
- **Agile as perfect or final.** The author favours Agile but explicitly says it is not the be-all and end-all. [AP] (Introduction, pp. 2–3, "Agile Isn’t Perfect")
- **A requirement-free development process.** Without explicit requirements, developers may optimise for personal interests, teams may diverge, stakeholders may pull the project toward fleeting preferences, and tracking and decision-making become harder. [AR] (Ch 3, pp. 32–33, "3.2 Why Requirements Matter")
- **UML notation as an end in itself.** Communication with the intended audience outranks perfect conformance; notation should remain basic or be explained, and another medium is preferable when it communicates more efficiently. [AR] (Ch 4, pp. 47–49, "4.2 What Diagrams Must Do Well"; "4.5 Why NOT Use UML?")
- **One architecture as universally best.** The monolith–microservice comparison repeatedly pairs advantages with costs, and the case study grounds the microservice choice in TOCS-specific deployment, data, technology, and configurability constraints. [AR] (Ch 5, pp. 61–67)
- **Prototype polish before high-level validation.** Low-fidelity paper prototypes are valuable precisely because they make large changes cheap; elaborate craft work is discouraged when a simpler sketch would communicate enough. [AR] (Ch 6, pp. 69–72)
- **Designing only for users like the designer.** The Inclusivity Heuristics require support across different risk attitudes, self-efficacy levels, information-processing styles, learning styles, and motivations. [AR] (Ch 7, pp. 73–83)
- **More comments as automatically better documentation.** Excessive comments can become stale, obscure important explanations, and signal code that should instead be simplified. [AR] (Ch 8, pp. 87–89)
- **Working code as sufficient reason not to refactor.** The chapter argues that poorly organised working code accumulates technical debt and can become increasingly costly to maintain. [AR] (Ch 8, p. 86, "8.1 Why Care about Code Smells?")
